item.title: Friday
item.description:
I haven’t got anything to add to today and I’m not going to pretend otherwise.

Everything’s cancelled. The strike that was meant to happen today was called off. The football’s gone for the weekend. The telly has been rearranged and everybody on it is speaking slower than usual.

I went out at lunch because I couldn’t sit still. There was a sign in a shop window, A4, in a plastic wallet, wording slightly off in the way things are when somebody has written it themselves rather than copied it from anywhere. There were a lot of those about.
item.content:
I haven’t got anything to add to today and I’m not going to pretend otherwise.

Everything’s cancelled. The strike that was meant to happen today was called off. The football’s gone for the weekend. The telly has been rearranged and everybody on it is speaking slower than usual.

I went out at lunch because I couldn’t sit still. There was a sign in a shop window, A4, in a plastic wallet, wording slightly off in the way things are when somebody has written it themselves rather than copied it from anywhere. There were a lot of those about.

Bought some milk. The woman on the till said “strange day”. I said “it is, isn’t it”. Neither of us said anything else, and that turned out to be exactly the right amount of talking.

That’s all I’ve got.

Back to normal service whenever normal service turns up.

item.title: Balmoral
item.description:
New Prime Minister officially took the job today, and it happened in Scotland, which apparently it never has before.

The handover normally goes on at Buckingham Palace. This time everybody flew up to Balmoral and did it there instead, because the Queen isn’t travelling much these days.

I find that I have no opinion whatsoever about this and I have been quietly enjoying that.

There’s a photograph of it that’s been absolutely everywhere today. She looks small, and rather cheerful about the whole business. Ninety six years old and still doing the job on a Tuesday.
item.content:
New Prime Minister officially took the job today, and it happened in Scotland, which apparently it never has before.

The handover normally goes on at Buckingham Palace. This time everybody flew up to Balmoral and did it there instead, because the Queen isn’t travelling much these days.

I find that I have no opinion whatsoever about this and I have been quietly enjoying that.

There’s a photograph of it that’s been absolutely everywhere today. She looks small, and rather cheerful about the whole business. Ninety six years old and still doing the job on a Tuesday.

Meanwhile the thing I’m actually waiting on is still somewhere over the horizon. Energy package, days away, possibly. Twenty five days until the cap.

In considerably smaller news, I have spent a week building a screen for my hallway and it has now taught me, on three separate occasions, that I design things for the chair I happen to be sitting in rather than the place they end up living.

Today’s instalment: I built a form for reporting that a fault is known about, which works beautifully at a desk, for a job that only ever happens while walking past something with your hands full.

I’m told this is called user research and that there are people who get paid for it. I have been doing it by building the wrong thing repeatedly and then walking past it.

Autumn’s properly settled in now. Jumper weather. The specific kind where you aren’t actually cold, you just fancy a jumper.

Twenty five days.

item.title: Monday
item.description:
So we have a new Prime Minister. I said on Friday that Monday would tell us, and Monday has duly told us.

I’m not going to do the politics.

Not because I haven’t got opinions. I have a full set and they’re available on request. It’s because this blog is three weeks old, I’d rather it didn’t turn into that, and because everybody else on the internet has today thoroughly covered at considerable length and increasing volume.
item.content:
So we have a new Prime Minister. I said on Friday that Monday would tell us, and Monday has duly told us.

I’m not going to do the politics.

Not because I haven’t got opinions. I have a full set and they’re available on request. It’s because this blog is three weeks old, I’d rather it didn’t turn into that, and because everybody else on the internet has today thoroughly covered at considerable length and increasing volume.

What I care about is October.

The cap lands on the first. Three thousand five hundred and forty nine pounds. That number has been sitting in my calendar since the twenty sixth of August doing nothing whatsoever except getting closer.

Word is there’s a support package coming within days. Might be enormous. Might be nothing much. Everybody has a theory, and everybody had a theory about the cap too, and every single one of those theories turned out to be wrong in both directions at once, so I have formally retired from theorising.

In the meantime the status page can now tell this house whether the internet is working, which is at least one question with a definite answer in it today.

Autumn’s properly here. The sun’s gone before eight now, which it wasn’t a fortnight ago. The wasps have gone quiet in a way I don’t entirely trust.

I’ll find out about October when everybody else does.

item.title: Fictional computers
item.description:
I have spent today establishing that the spaceship computers I have admired since I was a child would be completely useless to actually own.

Context, if you missed yesterday: I am building a status page for my house, and I have decided it ought to look like a Stargate console, for reasons that would not survive any sort of scrutiny.

So this morning I went and looked at one properly. Not fondly. Professionally, with every intention of stealing from it.
item.content:
I have spent today establishing that the spaceship computers I have admired since I was a child would be completely useless to actually own.

Context, if you missed yesterday: I am building a status page for my house, and I have decided it ought to look like a Stargate console, for reasons that would not survive any sort of scrutiny.

So this morning I went and looked at one properly. Not fondly. Professionally, with every intention of stealing from it.

They’re terrible. I’m sorry but they are genuinely terrible.

Everything is enormous. There are about four pieces of actual information on the entire screen. Half the elements are moving and don’t mean anything, because movement reads well on camera and stillness doesn’t. The whole thing is built to be legible to a lens for four seconds while somebody stands in front of it saying something important, and it has never once had to tell you eleven things at the same time, because no scene has ever needed it to.

Whereas a status page has to tell you eleven things at the same time, mostly in order to say that all eleven of them are fine.

So the rule for the rest of the day became: it should feel like the thing, not be the thing. Take the colours. Take the chunky edges. Absolutely take the typeface, that was forty minutes of my one life and I intend to get my money’s worth. But let the layout answer to the hallway rather than the director.

And then, having done all of that very cleverly, I put it on the screen in the hall and walked past it and could not read a single word.

I had built the entire thing sat at a desk with my face about sixty centimetres from a monitor. It lives in a corridor where people see it from three metres away, at an angle, while walking, usually carrying something in both hands.

Everything was too small. The contrast was perfectly fine at a desk and hopeless in a hallway with a window at one end. The most useful sentence on the whole page was sat exactly where your eye arrives last.

There is no clever technique for this. You go and stand where the person stands. That is the entire method, and apparently I need to be taught it again from scratch every single time.

Rebuilt for three metres. It’s uglier and enormously better.

The typeface survived. I’d like that noted.

Right. New Prime Minister tomorrow. Back to the real world in the morning.

item.title: Nobody asked for this
item.description:
I have started building something that nobody asked for, nobody needs, and which will take roughly four times as long as the sensible version, because I have decided it ought to look like a spaceship.

It’s a status page. For the house. A screen that tells everybody living here whether the films are working, whether the photos are working, and whether the internet is having one of its afternoons.

The useful version of this is a list. White background, green ticks, red crosses, finished by lunchtime, everybody gets on with their day.
item.content:
I have started building something that nobody asked for, nobody needs, and which will take roughly four times as long as the sensible version, because I have decided it ought to look like a spaceship.

It’s a status page. For the house. A screen that tells everybody living here whether the films are working, whether the photos are working, and whether the internet is having one of its afternoons.

The useful version of this is a list. White background, green ticks, red crosses, finished by lunchtime, everybody gets on with their day.

I am not building the useful version.

Every computer in this house is named after a Stargate episode and has been for years. There was never a realistic scenario in which I was going to build a screen for this house and then make it look like a normal screen. Chunky blue panels. Slightly too many lights. The general air of a room in which somebody is about to say “we’re picking up an energy signature”.

I spent forty minutes today choosing a typeface. Forty minutes. For a page that four people will ever look at, in a building where I could simply shout.

In my defence, and I would like a defence, it does solve something real. Nobody here ever tells me when something’s broken, because they don’t want to bother me, because I am perpetually doing something to the server. So the page will say when a thing is broken and also whether I already know about it, which means nobody ever has to stand there weighing up whether it’s worth mentioning.

That’s the justification. It’s a genuinely good justification.

It is not why I’m doing it.

Anyway. New Prime Minister on Monday, apparently. September is being extremely September about everything.

I’m going to go and have an argument with a colour picker.

item.title: Verdict is in
item.description:
September, then, and the verdict is in. Joint warmest summer on record for England. Seventeen point one degrees, level with 2018.

Which is an odd thing to read about a season you spent complaining your way through. All that moaning, and it turns out I was present at something.

So he wasn’t messing about after all. I owe Helios an apology, or at minimum an acknowledgement, which I’m perfectly willing to offer now that he’s gone.
item.content:
September, then, and the verdict is in. Joint warmest summer on record for England. Seventeen point one degrees, level with 2018.

Which is an odd thing to read about a season you spent complaining your way through. All that moaning, and it turns out I was present at something.

So he wasn’t messing about after all. I owe Helios an apology, or at minimum an acknowledgement, which I’m perfectly willing to offer now that he’s gone.

New Prime Minister on Monday. Whoever it turns out to be inherits October, which is four weeks out now and has a number attached to it.

The Treasury are apparently already drawing something up regardless, a mini budget within the fortnight. So the number might not end up being the number. I’m not going to get excited about that, having recently learned a certain amount about numbers, but I notice that I would quite like to.

It’s properly autumn out there today. Not cold. Just that light.

Anyway. Monday.

item.title: Gorbachev
item.description:
Tuesday behaving like a Monday, which is the going rate for a long weekend and I’d pay it again. Bins went out a day late. I watched from the window to check everyone else had got the memo, and they had, which was a small relief.

Gorbachev died today. Ninety one.

I have no memory of him at all. He isn’t history I lived through, he’s history that arrived in documentaries and other people’s anecdotes and that particular way older relatives say “when the Wall came down” as though you’d been standing next to them at the time.
item.content:
Tuesday behaving like a Monday, which is the going rate for a long weekend and I’d pay it again. Bins went out a day late. I watched from the window to check everyone else had got the memo, and they had, which was a small relief.

Gorbachev died today. Ninety one.

I have no memory of him at all. He isn’t history I lived through, he’s history that arrived in documentaries and other people’s anecdotes and that particular way older relatives say “when the Wall came down” as though you’d been standing next to them at the time.

What I keep snagging on is the timing of it. He’s the man who took the Cold War apart, and he’s gone and died six months into the whole thing being put back together, in a war he lived long enough to watch start. I don’t know what you’re meant to do with that. It doesn’t resolve into anything.

Apparently the obituaries here and the obituaries there describe two entirely different men, which I gather has been the case for about thirty years.

Posties out tomorrow.

Odd thing, being a bit sad about somebody you only ever knew as a fact.

item.title: the monday for sunday
item.description:
Bank holiday Monday, and that is the last one until Christmas.

I look this up every year, always on the day itself in the hope that I’ve misremembered it.

This year it’s sitting a bit differently, because what’s actually between here and Christmas is the winter, and the winter has been getting a great deal of advance press lately.

Anyways that’s a problem for October.

Today I had a bank holiday and I used it correctly, which is to say almost entirely horizontally. Somebody a few doors down has been barbecuing since roughly noon with genuine commitment. You can chart the whole arc of it from here without getting up. Optimistic start, long quiet middle, and then at about six a smell strongly suggesting things had got away from them.

It’s got that last-night-of-the-holidays feeling to it, which I do resent at my old age of 30. Bins tomorrow, a day late. Posties out again Wednesday. September on Thursday.

I’ll cope. I just wish somebody would space them out a bit.

item.title: the best sunday of the year
item.description:
Bank holiday Sunday, which is the best Sunday of the year on a technicality. All of the Sunday, none of the consequences. Tomorrow is somebody else’s problem and I am not required to be anywhere.

Everyone was out. Not doing anything especially, just out when the weather is behaving itself and there’s another day still to come. I like it out there on days like this but I don’t always.
item.content:
Bank holiday Sunday, which is the best Sunday of the year on a technicality. All of the Sunday, none of the consequences. Tomorrow is somebody else’s problem and I am not required to be anywhere.

Everyone was out. Not doing anything especially, just out when the weather is behaving itself and there’s another day still to come. I like it out there on days like this but I don’t always.

It’s the last Sunday of August, which I feel rather more than seems reasonable. I get the distinct sense of something being quietly packed away.

Wasps were quiet today, incidentally. Either they’ve moved on or they’re regrouping.

I’ve decided not to look into it.

item.title: Bank Holiday weekend
item.description:
Bank holiday weekend, so three whole days in which to not think about it, and I fully intended to use all of them.

Made it to about half ten.

It isn’t dread, It’s arithmetic. You catch yourself doing sums you never sat down to do, in the queue, filling the kettle, halfway up the stairs, and then you put them away again and they come back later having brought friends.
item.content:
Bank holiday weekend, so three whole days in which to not think about it, and I fully intended to use all of them.

Made it to about half ten.

It isn’t dread, It’s arithmetic. You catch yourself doing sums you never sat down to do, in the queue, filling the kettle, halfway up the stairs, and then you put them away again and they come back later having brought friends.

Right, enough of that.

The wasps have escalated. One got into the kitchen this afternoon and conducted itself like something with a grievance and a list. I did the thing where you open every window in the room and then stand very still in the corner, narrating your own reasonableness at it in a low voice.

It left of its own accord in the end, having made its point. I’m still not clear what the point was.

Shops were heaving. Everybody buying the same disposable barbecue and the same four bags of ice with the confidence of people who have not checked the forecast and would prefer not to be told.

Bin day’s shifted because of Monday. Posties out again Wednesday.

That’s the shape of the week ahead and, all things considered, I’ll take it.

item.title: Price Cap
item.description:
Didn’t write Wednesday or Thursday. Helios turned up in the end, roughly on schedule, and I notice I’ve stopped keeping track of him.

£3,549.

There it is, then. Up from £1,971. Eighty per cent in one step, from the first of October.

I said last weekend that I wasn’t going to look at any of the predictions on the grounds that I’d find out on Friday either way and I’d like to report back that knowing is not better. I had been carrying it about as a shape, and now it’s a figure, and the figure is worse than the shape was.
item.content:
Didn’t write Wednesday or Thursday. Helios turned up in the end, roughly on schedule, and I notice I’ve stopped keeping track of him.

£3,549.

There it is, then. Up from £1,971. Eighty per cent in one step, from the first of October.

I said last weekend that I wasn’t going to look at any of the predictions on the grounds that I’d find out on Friday either way and I’d like to report back that knowing is not better. I had been carrying it about as a shape, and now it’s a figure, and the figure is worse than the shape was.

Then underneath it, almost in passing, the forecasts for next year are sitting somewhere around six thousand eight hundred. This is the bad news arriving early to make room for the worse news behind it.

The library thing makes considerably more sense to me now than it did on Sunday.

Posties out today as well, a hundred and fifteen thousand of them, first of four days on strike. Everyone is asking for more money because everything costs more money, and I’m not sure what anybody imagined would happen instead.

It’s still warm out but its not unbearably warm, which makes it a shame that of this landed on a perfectly nice afternoon.

Anyway. Nothing left to count down to.

item.title: Wasps
item.description:
The wasps have started, the proper late August asshole wasps.

I finally looked up why they turn like this, because it happens every single year and I’ve never known. Turns out the colony is basically finished by now. The queen has stopped laying, so there are no grubs left to feed, and it was the grubs that produced the sugary stuff the workers lived on. So the workers have no job and no income and they go off hunting sugar wherever they can find it, which is your pint, and the bin, and the windfall apples fermenting quietly in the grass.
item.content:
The wasps have started, the proper late August asshole wasps.

I finally looked up why they turn like this, because it happens every single year and I’ve never known. Turns out the colony is basically finished by now. The queen has stopped laying, so there are no grubs left to feed, and it was the grubs that produced the sugary stuff the workers lived on. So the workers have no job and no income and they go off hunting sugar wherever they can find it, which is your pint, and the bin, and the windfall apples fermenting quietly in the grass.

They are, in short, unemployed and drunk and furious about it.

I have never felt closer to them.

Warm today, properly warm. Tomorrow is meant to be the twenty eight. I’ll believe that when it happens, but I have carefully made no plans that would stop me sitting in it.

It’s dark before nine now, which it wasn’t a fortnight ago. That one always gets me. You don’t notice it going and then one evening you look up and the day has simply ended without checking with you first.

The shops have moved on regardless. Pencil cases where the barbecue things were.

Three days.

item.title: GCSEs
item.description:
Monday, and the first properly warm one since he came back. Not twenty eight yet. Building up to it slowly, like he wants us to notice the effort involved.

There’s an education person in the paper today explaining that girls will do better than boys in this week’s GCSEs because the girls revised during lockdown and the boys played PlayStation.

I have read this three times now and it has not improved.
item.content:
Monday, and the first properly warm one since he came back. Not twenty eight yet. Building up to it slowly, like he wants us to notice the effort involved.

There’s an education person in the paper today explaining that girls will do better than boys in this week’s GCSEs because the girls revised during lockdown and the boys played PlayStation.

I have read this three times now and it has not improved.

I would like to register, from a safe distance of some years, that it is entirely possible to do both. I did both. Simultaneously, on occasion, which I appreciate is not the same as doing either of them well.

The other possibility, which the piece does not trouble itself with, is that a cohort sitting their first real exams after two years of not having any might produce results that resist one tidy explanation. But that won’t go in a headline. PlayStation goes in a headline.

Elsewhere, and considerably less funny, something like 1.7 million households are reckoning on cancelling their energy direct debits. Not switching, not haggling, not ringing up to complain. Cancelling. Which tells you fairly precisely where we’ve got to, four days out. Its a great time to work for an energy company, sigh.

Twenty eight on Wednesday, then. Three days of being pleased about the weather, and then Friday, and then I expect we all go a bit quiet for a while.

item.title: Shapps
item.description:
Trains today, in the loose sense that some of them happened.

Shapps is telling the RMT to put the eight per cent to a vote, and the RMT are telling him where he can put it instead, so I imagine we’ll all be doing this again shortly.

Read something at breakfast that I’ve not been able to put down since. Libraries and museums are working out whether they can operate as warm places this winter, for people who won’t be putting the heating on. Not as a campaign, or a stunt, or a point anybody is making. As a plan. They’re asking for money to do it properly.
item.content:
Trains today, in the loose sense that some of them happened.

Shapps is telling the RMT to put the eight per cent to a vote, and the RMT are telling him where he can put it instead, so I imagine we’ll all be doing this again shortly.

Read something at breakfast that I’ve not been able to put down since. Libraries and museums are working out whether they can operate as warm places this winter, for people who won’t be putting the heating on. Not as a campaign, or a stunt, or a point anybody is making. As a plan. They’re asking for money to do it properly.

I keep picking it up and turning it over and not getting anywhere useful with it. It’s such a practical, sensible, kind thing for a library to decide to be. The bit I can’t get past is that it needs deciding.

Further down the same list of the day’s news, it’s going to be twenty eight degrees on Wednesday. Warmer than Mexico City, apparently, which is the comparison papers reach for once they’ve exhausted the other ways of saying hot.

So he’s back after all. I withdraw what I said about him yesterday, he was evidently just running late.

It’s a strange pair of things to be holding on the same Sunday, though. Twenty eight on Wednesday, and a library somewhere working out how many chairs it can put out in January.

Fun fact, none of this actually affects me because my job is Work-From-Home and has been since Covid. I don’t miss the commute but I do miss the routine of the office, can’t have one without the other.

Anyway. Cap on Friday.

item.title: Strike day
item.description:
Strike day, so no trains, so I have spent Saturday entirely within walking distance of my own front door.

I want to be clear that I support them completely and also that I had plans.

It’s the signallers that do it. Network Rail are out alongside most of the operators, and once the signallers go it stops mattering who else fancied coming in, the whole thing simply stops working. Thursday they managed about a fifth of the network. Today felt like rather less than that, though I’m going off the app and a general atmosphere rather than anything rigorous.
item.content:
Strike day, so no trains, so I have spent Saturday entirely within walking distance of my own front door.

I want to be clear that I support them completely and also that I had plans.

It’s the signallers that do it. Network Rail are out alongside most of the operators, and once the signallers go it stops mattering who else fancied coming in, the whole thing simply stops working. Thursday they managed about a fifth of the network. Today felt like rather less than that, though I’m going off the app and a general atmosphere rather than anything rigorous.

The one nice part, and I wouldn’t say this to anybody actually striking, is that it’s quiet out there in a way a Saturday never usually is. No day trippers. Everyone who did make it out was on foot and had visibly decided to be cheerful about it, which I found unexpectedly nice to be around.

Ofgem announce the new cap on Friday. Everybody has a number they’re passing about, all of them different, all of them somehow worse than the last one you heard. Nobody actually knows yet, which has not slowed anyone down in the slightest. I’ve decided not to look at any of the predictions, on the grounds that I’ll find out on Friday either way and there is nothing useful to be done with six days of advance dread except sit and have it.

I have of course looked at all of them.

No sign of Helios either, incidentally. I said last time he was due back this week and he has simply not turned up, which after all that fuss I am choosing to take personally.

So it’s been an indoors day, doing the category of job you only ever get to when you can’t leave the house. The sort where you finish, and the room looks precisely the same as it did before, and you’re somehow tired.

Anyway. Trains on Monday, allegedly.

item.title: Heat broke
item.description:
The heat broke on Sunday and I’ve been in a funny mood about it ever since.

I spent most of last week complaining loudly to anybody who would stand still for it that it was too hot to function. Then Helios packed it in, wandered off to bother somebody else, and now it’s nineteen degrees and grey and I find that I miss him. Not enough to want him back but still enough to be annoyed about it.
item.content:
The heat broke on Sunday and I’ve been in a funny mood about it ever since.

I spent most of last week complaining loudly to anybody who would stand still for it that it was too hot to function. Then Helios packed it in, wandered off to bother somebody else, and now it’s nineteen degrees and grey and I find that I miss him. Not enough to want him back but still enough to be annoyed about it.

Monday through Wednesday it hammered it down, which the ground was in no fit state to deal with. That rain that just sits on top of the soil looking at you whereas down south they got proper flooding out of it, sewage on the beaches, warnings, the lot. We got puddles and a smell.

Meanwhile eight parts of England are now officially in drought and we, up here, are not. No hosepipe ban either. I have never in my life been so proud of something I had absolutely no involvement in.

Although.

The Pennine reservoirs are sitting at about half full when they’d usually be three quarters, and Dovestone currently looks like somebody’s pulled the plug out of it. So I think what’s actually happened is that we are in a drought and simply haven’t been informed on the grounds that half the region drinks Lake District rain and the Lake District has never had a dry week in its entire life.

I went up to have a look at our reservoir on Wednesday. In the rain. Like a normal person.

Still working out what this blog is for, incidentally. I had assumed I’d have a theme by now. Instead I have the weather, which is arguably a theme, just not a good one.

Forecast says he’s back next week. Low twenties, nothing dramatic. Which is the correct amount of sun, and therefore nobody will mention it at all.

item.title: Hello
item.description:
After walking nearly three miles into Chorlton during the hottest heatwave of the year, losing ninety-percent of my body’s mass through sweat, I got most of it back by getting drenched in a monsoon-like deluge on the way back.

And with that intro out of the way, now I’m launching my dailyblog. Yes, a dailyblog. How very early 2000s of me.

Since I’m cheap, I’m hosting it on GitHub.io, but its also because I’m not brave enough to publish it on any of the pile of the domains I own, call me an extroverted-introvert if you want.

item.title: Links
item.description:
The web is better when people link to each other. Here’s what I read and where else I exist.

Mine

  • cozyhousecat.github.io — the main site

Homelab and self-hosting

  • Proxmox VE docs — genuinely good reference
  • Awesome Selfhosted — the canonical list
  • Anubis — proof-of-work bot deterrence

Tools I’d miss

  • Hugo — this site
  • re-Terminal — this theme

Got a site? Tell me about it and I’ll take a look.
